question.prompt: What kind of rain is the Cloudpocket cape designed to resist?
question.explanation: The important details explicitly limit the cape to light showers. The broader headline cannot replace the stated design limitation.

stimulus.title: An advertisement with small print
stimulus.body:
THE CLOUDPOCKET: A DRY JOURNEY STARTS HERE!

Our new folding rain cape fits into its own pocket. At only 180 grams, it can travel in a school bag without taking the place of your lunch. Reflective strips help other people notice the wearer in low light. Choose from three colours. Order this week for a free storage pouch.

Important details: the cape resists light showers. It is not designed for prolonged heavy rain. Reflective strips do not produce their own light and do not replace appropriate road safety behaviour. The free pouch offer ends on Sunday and applies while stocks last. Delivery charges are additional.

A class comparing advertisements noticed that the large headline suggested a broad benefit, while the small print narrowed the conditions. The cape might suit a short walk in changeable weather. A buyer planning a long hike would need information beyond the headline. The class decided that useful reading meant bringing the two parts together, rather than trusting the largest words or dismissing the product because it had limitations.

workedSolution: The important details explicitly limit the cape to light showers.
The broader headline cannot replace the stated design limitation.

question.prompt: What object does Elsie bring to the museum?
question.explanation: The opening identifies Elsie's contribution as the button. Her brother brings the programme, while the coat and torch appear in recollections.

stimulus.title: The museum drawer
stimulus.body:
The museum asked residents to bring objects connected with the old picture theatre. Elsie brought a brass button. Her brother brought a programme with a date printed on its cover.

'The button came from the usher's coat,' Elsie said. 'I remember its blue wool.'

Her brother frowned. 'The coats were green.'

They were certain of different colours, but agreed about the torch the usher used to guide late arrivals. The curator recorded both memories beside the button. She placed the dated programme in a separate sleeve.

'Which of us is right?' Elsie asked.

'I do not know yet,' the curator replied. 'A photograph may help. Your memories still tell us how the theatre mattered to you, even where they differ.'

When the display opened, visitors saw the button, the programme and two short recollections. A small card asked whether anyone had a clear photograph of an usher's coat. Elsie smiled at the card. Her memory had not been discarded, but neither had it become a fact merely because she remembered it vividly.

workedSolution: The opening identifies Elsie's contribution as the button.
Her brother brings the programme, while the coat and torch appear in recollections.
reviewFocus: Independently solve without the key; check each alternative and the stated conditions.
Review originality, vocabulary, difficulty and time for an above-average Year 5/6 learner.

stimulus.title: Who uses the oval?
stimulus.body:
Two suggestions reached the school council about the oval. One group wanted permanent football goals. Another wanted a marked walking loop. The council asked pupils to observe how the oval was used at three different times each day for a week.

At lunch, football players occupied most of the centre. Before school, smaller groups walked around the edge. After school, the oval was often empty, though on two afternoons a sports club trained there. The observers noted that pupils waiting for friends sometimes stood where a proposed walking loop would run.

The council rejected the idea that the most visible activity must be the only important one. It recommended movable goals and a trial walking route marked with cones. This would preserve options while revealing whether the activities interfered with each other. The recommendation did not give every group everything it wanted. It gave the school a way to learn before fixing equipment permanently in place.
